questions.question:
**In the following question, some part of the sentence may have errors. Find out which part of the sentence has an error and select the appropriate option. If a sentence is free from errors, select 'No Error'.** 

She is walking (1)/ in the park (2)/ since morning. (3)/ No error (4)
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **1**, i.e., *'She is walking'*

* [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__***

__
 
• It is clear through the word '**since'** that the walking began in the morning and is still ongoing.
 
• In such cases, **present perfect continuous tense** is used since it is an action that is continuing in the present.

**Thus the correct sentence is: ***She has been walking in the park since morning.*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Please refer to the following table for the types of tenses and their uses
 
 
 

 **Tense**
 **Functions**
 **Example**
 
 

 Present simple
 used for facts, generalizations, and truths that are not affected by the passage of time
 “She **writes **a lot of papers for her classes.”
 
 

 Past simple
 used for events completed in the past
 “She **wrote** the papers for all of her classes last month.”
 
 

 Future simple
 used for events to be completed in the future
 “She **will write** papers for her classes next semester.”
 
 

 Present perfect
 used to describe events that began in the past and are expected to continue, or to emphasize the relevance of past events to the present moment
 “She **has written** papers for most of her classes, but she still has some papers left to write.”
 
 

 Past perfect
 used to describe events that happened prior to other events in the past
 “She **had written** several papers for her classes before she switched universities.”
 
 

 Future perfect
 used to describe events that will be completed between now and a specific point in the future
 “She **will have written** many papers for her classes by the end of the semester.”
 
 

 Present continuous
 used to describe currently ongoing (usually temporary) actions
 “She **is writing** a paper for her class.”
 
 

 Past continuous
 used to describe ongoing past events, often in relation to the occurrence of another event
 “She **was writing** a paper for her class when her pencil broke.”
 
 

 Future continuous
 used to describe future events that are expected to continue over a period of time
 “She **will be writing** a lot of papers for her classes next year.”
 
 

 Present perfect continuous
 used to describe events that started in the past and continue into the present or were recently completed, emphasizing their relevance to the present moment
 “She **has been writing** a paper all night, and now she needs to get some sleep.”
 
 

 Past perfect continuous
 used to describe events that began, continued, and ended in the past, emphasizing their relevance to a past moment
 “She **had been writing **a paper all night, and she needed to get some sleep.”
 
 

 Future perfect continuous
 used to describe events that will continue up until a point in the future, emphasizing their expected duration
 “She **will have been writing** this paper for three months when she hands it in.”

questions.question: Trypsin is present in which of the following?
questions.solution:

__
 
• The pancreas secretes a liquid substance called** pancreatic juice**, which contains digestive enzymes.
 
• Trypsinogen, chymotrypsinogen, procarboxypeptidases, amylases, lipases, and nucleases are among the inactive enzymes found in the pancreatic juice secreted by the pancreas.
 
• These enzymes help in the breakdown of all food components that require digestion.
 
• **Enterokinase**, an enzyme secreted by the intestinal mucosa, converts trypsinogen into active trypsin.
 
• **Trypsin **helps to convert proteins into peptones.
 
• **Chymotrypsinogen** is a degrading enzyme that breaks down proteins into smaller peptides.
 
• **Procarboxypeptidases** enzymes remove C-terminal amino acids from peptides and proteins
 
• **Amylase **enzyme converts starch to maltose.
 
• **Lipase** is a digestive enzyme that breaks down fats into glycerol and fatty acids.
 
• **Nucleases** enzymes are specifically designed to break down the nucleotides that make up DNA and RNA.

**Conclusion:**__

**Trypsin **is found in the digestive system. It hydrolyzes proteins. It is present in the pancreatic juice and formed in the small intestine.

questions.question: The power of an earthquake is expressed in terms of a magnitude on a scale called ________ scale.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is** Richter**

**CONCEPT:**

__
 
• **The power of an earthquake is expressed in terms of a magnitude on a scale called the Richter scale.**__
 
• The Richter scale was developed by Charles F. Richter and is used to measure the strength or magnitude of an earthquake.

__Explanation:__

Earthquake: An earthquake is a sudden shaking or trembling of the earth which lasts for a very short time. It is caused by a disturbance deep inside the earth’s crust.

 
• An earthquake is measured with a machine called a seismograph. The power of an earthquake is expressed in terms of magnitude on a scale called the Richter scale.
 
• An earthquake of 2.0 or less can be felt only a little.
 
• An earthquake over 5.0 can cause damage from things falling.
 
• A 6.0 or higher magnitude is considered very strong and 7.0 is classified as a major earthquake.
 
• Really destructive earthquakes have magnitudes higher than 7 on the Richter scale.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/14a95093f70204497d807bd98ba9be1318ae24b1c5852285fd197a44adb02aa2.png] 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/68a5f7892446d2db1ea92192e705e47a9f7764c05df8b751eee8cc23d4b3a3d1.png] 

 
• Richter scale is not linear. This means that an earthquake of magnitude 6 does not have one and a half times the destructive energy of an earthquake of magnitude 4.
 
• In fact, an increase of 2 in magnitude means 1000 times more destructive energy. Therefore, an earthquake of magnitude 6 has a thousand times more destructive energy than an earthquake of magnitude 4.
